title: Dante's journey
hookLine: midway through life's journey, lost in a dark wood, Dante is led by love through hell, purgatory and heaven
carry: the love that moves the sun

cards: In the middle of the journey of our life, I found myself in a dark wood, for the straight way was lost. That's how a long Christian poem begins, put into plain English.
A man halfway through his life wakes up lost, with no idea how he got there. The wood is wild and thick. He sees a hill with sunlight on it and tries to climb, and wild animals drive him back down.
He is stuck. Then someone appears to help. The man is the poet Dante, writing about himself.

teach.b: The poem is known as the Divine Comedy. The help that comes in the wood is the ghost of Virgil, an old Roman poet, sent because Beatrice, a woman Dante loved who has died, asked for him.
So the journey starts with love reaching down into the dark. Virgil leads Dante down through hell, where people are stuck forever in the shape of their choices.
Then up a mountain, purgatory, where souls are being healed and made ready, climbing slowly, even singing. Then Beatrice herself guides him up through the heavens.
The way out of the dark wood isn't straight up the sunny hill.
It goes down first, and only then up. The poem is honest about pain. In heaven, Dante's ancestor tells him what's coming: he'll be driven out of his city, Florence.
He'll learn how salty another man's bread tastes, and how hard it is to climb another man's stairs. Then the last line. Dante sees God, and can't describe it.
All he can say is that his desire and will were turned, like a wheel, by "l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle."

teach.h: THE LOVE THAT MOVES THE SUN.
teach.b: The love that moves the sun and the other stars. The poem began in a dark wood. It ends at the center of everything, with love.
Christians read it in different ways: as a story, a map of the soul, a vision.

how: Christians and other readers take up Dante's Divine Comedy as poetry and as a spiritual journey, and some churches and reading groups go through it slowly, a canto at a time.

o: a knight's long quest for a lost holy cup
a poem's road from a dark wood, through hell, to heaven
a pilgrim's walk from Florence to Rome for Easter

p: led him through hell and purgatory

s: Dante escapes the dark wood by climbing the sunny hill
wild animals drive him back. the way out goes down first, then up.
Virgil guides Dante all the way into heaven
Virgil leads him through hell and up the mountain of purgatory. Beatrice guides him through the heavens.
the poem's last line speaks of love
the love that moves the sun and the other stars.

games.q: you're Dante, lost in a dark wood. you see a hill with sunlight on it. what do you do?
o: climb straight up toward the light.
games.why: he tries to climb, and wild animals drive him back. help comes, and the way out turns out to go down first, then up.

practice: Ask quietly where you are on your own journey, in a dark wood, going down through something hard, climbing slowly, or somewhere bright, and name it in a word or two, with nothing to fix.
Then ask who has been your Virgil, someone who helped you find the way. If you pray, bring that place and that person to God; if not, hold them both for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Dante's journey. A poet lost in a dark wood, led by love down through hell, up the mountain of purgatory, and into heaven.

carryVoice: Your line: the love that moves the sun. The dark wood was only the beginning. On to tomorrow.
